In short, size normalisation removes the mean-degree confound and confirms that the modularity-based claim of stronger community structure in Aur-P1 survives net of network size, whereas neither phase's mean degree can be used as evidence of intrinsically higher connectivity.

## S5.10 Multiple Regression on Distance Matrices (Drivers of Sign Dissimilarity) {#sec-s5-10}

The Mantel tests establish that geographic distance is not significantly correlated with sign dissimilarity in either phase, but a non-significant result cannot by itself identify which alternative process — if any — generated the pattern. To split the variance of sign dissimilarity among the candidate drivers that are actually measured in the data, we fit a multiple regression on distance matrices (MRM; @Lichstein_2007) in which the response is the Jaccard dissimilarity of sign presence/absence and the three predictors are, for every pair of sites, their geographic distance, their absolute temporal distance (|ΔMedianBP|), and their absolute difference in object count (a proxy for sampling effort). Each predictor is entered as a distance matrix so that all three are placed on a common pairwise footing. We fit the model separately for Aur-P1 and Aur-P2 to mirror the phase-specific Mantel tests, and we report the coefficient, permutation p-value, and 95% bootstrap confidence interval for each driver.

```{r}
#| label: s5-10-mrm
#| warning: false

mrm_phase <- function(art, uniq, nperm = 10000, B = 500) {
  sites <- uniq   # rows are assumed aligned with the rows of art
  Y   <- as.dist(vegan::vegdist(art, method = "jaccard", binary = TRUE))
  pts <- sites %>% sf::st_as_sf(coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326)
  geo <- sf::st_distance(pts) %>% as.dist()
  temp <- dist(sites$MedianBP)
  obj  <- dist(sites$nobjects)
  fit <- MRM(Y ~ geo + temp + obj, nperm = nperm)
  set.seed(7)
  boot_one <- function() {
    idx <- sample(nrow(art), replace = TRUE)
    Yb  <- as.dist(vegan::vegdist(art[idx, ], method = "jaccard", binary = TRUE))
    pb  <- sites[idx, , drop = FALSE] %>% sf::st_as_sf(coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326)
    gb  <- sf::st_distance(pb) %>% as.dist()
    tb  <- dist(sites$MedianBP[idx])
    ob  <- dist(sites$nobjects[idx])
    res <- tryCatch(MRM(Yb ~ gb + tb + ob, nperm = 10)$coef,
                    error = function(e) NULL)
    if (is.null(res) || !("Y" %in% colnames(res))) return(NULL)
    if (any(is.na(res[, "Y"]))) return(NULL)
    res[, "Y"]
  }
  boots <- replicate(B, boot_one(), simplify = FALSE)
  boots <- boots[!sapply(boots, is.null)]
  boots <- do.call(cbind, boots)
  list(coef   = fit$coef,
       r2     = fit$r.squared,
       geo_ci = quantile(boots["geo", ], c(0.025, 0.975)),
       temp_ci= quantile(boots["temp", ], c(0.025, 0.975)),
       obj_ci = quantile(boots["obj", ],  c(0.025, 0.975)))
}

mrm_p1 <- mrm_phase(aurp1_artifact_data, aurp1_unique_data)
mrm_p2 <- mrm_phase(aurp2_artifact_data, aurp2_unique_data)

mrm_p1_r2 <- mrm_p1$r.squared
mrm_p2_r2 <- mrm_p2$r.squared

mrm_p1_geo <- mrm_p1$coef["geo","Y"]; mrm_p1_geo_p <- mrm_p1$coef["geo","pval"]
mrm_p1_geo_lo <- mrm_p1$geo_ci[1]; mrm_p1_geo_hi <- mrm_p1$geo_ci[2]
mrm_p1_temp <- mrm_p1$coef["temp","Y"]; mrm_p1_temp_p <- mrm_p1$coef["temp","pval"]
mrm_p1_temp_lo <- mrm_p1$temp_ci[1]; mrm_p1_temp_hi <- mrm_p1$temp_ci[2]
mrm_p1_obj <- mrm_p1$coef["obj","Y"]; mrm_p1_obj_p <- mrm_p1$coef["obj","pval"]
mrm_p1_obj_lo <- mrm_p1$obj_ci[1]; mrm_p1_obj_hi <- mrm_p1$obj_ci[2]

mrm_p2_geo <- mrm_p2$coef["geo","Y"]; mrm_p2_geo_p <- mrm_p2$coef["geo","pval"]
mrm_p2_temp <- mrm_p2$coef["temp","Y"]; mrm_p2_temp_p <- mrm_p2$coef["temp","pval"]
mrm_p2_obj <- mrm_p2$coef["obj","Y"]; mrm_p2_obj_p <- mrm_p2$coef["obj","pval"]
mrm_p2_geo_lo <- mrm_p2$geo_ci[1]; mrm_p2_geo_hi <- mrm_p2$geo_ci[2]
mrm_p2_temp_lo <- mrm_p2$temp_ci[1]; mrm_p2_temp_hi <- mrm_p2$temp_ci[2]
mrm_p2_obj_lo <- mrm_p2$obj_ci[1]; mrm_p2_obj_hi <- mrm_p2$obj_ci[2]
```

For Aur-P1 the MRM explains `r n2(mrm_p1_r2)` of the variance in sign dissimilarity; none of the three drivers is significant (geographic: β = `r n3(mrm_p1_geo)`, 95% CI [`r n3(mrm_p1_geo_lo)`, `r n3(mrm_p1_geo_hi)`], p = `r n3(mrm_p1_geo_p)`; temporal: β = `r n3(mrm_p1_temp)`, 95% CI [`r n3(mrm_p1_temp_lo)`, `r n3(mrm_p1_temp_hi)`], p = `r n3(mrm_p1_temp_p)`; object count: β = `r n3(mrm_p1_obj)`, 95% CI [`r n3(mrm_p1_obj_lo)`, `r n3(mrm_p1_obj_hi)`], p = `r n3(mrm_p1_obj_p)`). Aur-P2 shows the same pattern (R² = `r n2(mrm_p2_r2)`; geographic p = `r n3(mrm_p2_geo_p)`, temporal p = `r n3(mrm_p2_temp_p)`, object-count p = `r n3(mrm_p2_obj_p)`). Because no candidate driver reaches significance, the non-significant Mantel result does not identify any particular alternative process: it is consistent with several possibilities — including non-utilitarian mobility, aggregation, or independent invention — but demonstrates none of them. With only `r nrow(aurp2_artifact_data)` sites, the Aur-P2 MRM is underpowered, so its non-significant coefficients should be read as indicative rather than conclusive; the substantive point is that the data contain no statistical evidence favouring one driver over another.

## S5.11 Mantel Correlogram and Bootstrap Confidence Intervals on the Mantel R {#sec-s5-11}

### Rationale

The Mantel tests reported in the main text and in S3 evaluate a single global null hypothesis: that geometric-sign dissimilarity is uncorrelated with geographic distance across all site pairs simultaneously. A non-significant global result can conceal scale-dependent structure — for example, sign sharing might be geographically clustered at short distances but random at long distances, producing a net correlation near zero. Because the global test cannot distinguish "no spatial structure at any scale" from "positive and negative structure that cancel," we ask two specific questions:

1. **Does sign dissimilarity show any spatial autocorrelation at a specific distance lag?** A Mantel correlogram partitions site pairs by geographic-distance bin and tests the Mantel correlation within each bin; a significant positive r at one or more lags would reveal scale-dependent structure that the global test misses.
2. **How uncertain is the global Mantel R estimate, and what does that imply about statistical power?** We place a bootstrap 95% confidence interval on the single global Mantel R reported for each phase. A wide interval that overlaps zero indicates the test cannot distinguish a true null from a true moderate correlation, so the non-significant result is a lack of evidence rather than evidence of absence.

### Analysis

We reconstruct, for each phase, the Jaccard sign dissimilarity and the geodesic geographic-distance matrix used by the S3 Mantel tests (the same construction as `run_mantel_comp`, applied to the technology-assigned phase data). The Mantel correlogram is computed with `ecodist::mgram`, which bins pairs by geographic distance — into 5 equiprobable lags for Aur-P1 and 3 for Aur-P2, to keep pair counts per lag stable given the small samples — and returns the Mantel r, a permutation p-value, and 95% bootstrap confidence limits (llim/ulim) for each lag. For the global statistic we additionally resample sites with replacement (B = 1000) and recompute the Mantel R each time, taking the 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles as the bootstrap interval.

```{r}
#| label: s5-11-mantel-corr
#| warning: false

phase_distances <- function(df) {
  art <- df %>%
    dplyr::select(line:star) %>%
    dplyr::select(where(~ is.numeric(.) && sum(.) != 0)) %>%
    mutate(across(everything(), ~ as.numeric(. > 0)))
  jac <- vegan::vegdist(art, "jaccard", binary = TRUE)
  sf_obj <- sf::st_as_sf(df, coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326)
  geo <- as.dist(sf::st_distance(sf_obj) / 1000)
  list(jac = jac, geo = geo)
}

pd_p1 <- phase_distances(aurp1_unique_data)
pd_p2 <- phase_distances(aurp2_unique_data)

nclass_p1 <- 5
nclass_p2 <- 3
set.seed(2024)

mg_p1 <- ecodist::mgram(pd_p1$jac, pd_p1$geo,
                        nclass = nclass_p1, equiprobable = TRUE,
                        nboot = 1000, cboot = 0.95, nperm = 1000)
mg_p2 <- ecodist::mgram(pd_p2$jac, pd_p2$geo,
                        nclass = nclass_p2, equiprobable = TRUE,
                        nboot = 1000, cboot = 0.95, nperm = 1000)

mg_p1_df <- as.data.frame(mg_p1$mgram) %>% mutate(Phase = "Aur-P1")
mg_p2_df <- as.data.frame(mg_p2$mgram) %>% mutate(Phase = "Aur-P2")
mg_plot_df <- bind_rows(mg_p1_df, mg_p2_df)

# Global Mantel R (point estimate + permutation p), same construction as S3
mp1 <- vegan::mantel(pd_p1$geo, pd_p1$jac, permutations = 1000)
mp2 <- vegan::mantel(pd_p2$geo, pd_p2$jac, permutations = 1000)
mg_p1_r <- mp1$statistic; mg_p1_p <- mp1$signif
mg_p2_r <- mp2$statistic; mg_p2_p <- mp2$signif

# Bootstrap 95% CI on the global Mantel R via site resampling
boot_mantel_R <- function(df, B = 1000, seed = 42) {
  set.seed(seed); n <- nrow(df); Rs <- numeric(B)
  for (b in seq_len(B)) {
    pd <- phase_distances(df[sample(seq_len(n), n, replace = TRUE), ])
    Rs[b] <- vegan::mantel(pd$geo, pd$jac, permutations = 0)$statistic
  }
  quantile(Rs, c(0.025, 0.975))
}
mb_p1 <- boot_mantel_R(aurp1_unique_data)
mb_p2 <- boot_mantel_R(aurp2_unique_data)
mb_p1_lo <- mb_p1[1]; mb_p1_hi <- mb_p1[2]
mb_p2_lo <- mb_p2[1]; mb_p2_hi <- mb_p2[2]

n_pairs_p1 <- nrow(aurp1_unique_data) * (nrow(aurp1_unique_data) - 1) / 2
n_pairs_p2 <- nrow(aurp2_unique_data) * (nrow(aurp2_unique_data) - 1) / 2
```

```{r fig.height=5, fig.width=8}
#| label: fig-mantel-correlogram
#| fig-cap: "Mantel correlogram of geometric-sign dissimilarity against geographic distance, by phase. Points are the Mantel r within each distance lag; error bars are 95% bootstrap confidence intervals (ecodist::mgram, llim/ulim). The dashed line is r = 0. No lag reaches significance, and all intervals straddle zero."

ggplot(mg_plot_df, aes(x = lag, y = mantelr)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, colour = "#2c7fb8") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = llim, ymax = ulim), width = 0.08, colour = "#2c7fb8") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  facet_wrap(~ Phase, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = "Geographic distance lag (km)", y = "Mantel r") +
  theme_minimal()
```

### Interpretation

**Question 1 — is there scale-dependent spatial structure?** No. In Aur-P1 the `r nclass_p1` distance lags yield Mantel r values from `r n3(min(mg_p1_df$mantelr))` to `r n3(max(mg_p1_df$mantelr))`, none significant (smallest p = `r n3(min(mg_p1_df$pval))`); in Aur-P2 the `r nclass_p2` lags range from `r n3(min(mg_p2_df$mantelr))` to `r n3(max(mg_p2_df$mantelr))`, also none significant (smallest p = `r n3(min(mg_p2_df$pval))`). Every lag's 95% bootstrap interval straddles or lies close to zero: the most extreme bounds across lags are `r n3(min(mg_p1_df$llim))` and `r n3(max(mg_p1_df$ulim))` for Aur-P1 and `r n3(min(mg_p2_df$llim))` and `r n3(max(mg_p2_df$ulim))` for Aur-P2, both comfortably including zero. The correlogram is flat and structureless at every scale, so the global non-significant result is not masking a hidden short-range or long-range signal: sign dissimilarity is uncorrelated with geographic distance at all distance lags in both phases.

**Question 2 — how uncertain is the global R, and what does this say about power?** The global Mantel R is `r n3(mg_p1_r)` (p = `r n3(mg_p1_p)`) for Aur-P1 and `r n3(mg_p2_r)` (p = `r n3(mg_p2_p)`) for Aur-P2, matching the S3 geodesic results. The bootstrap 95% CI on this statistic is [`r n3(mb_p1_lo)`, `r n3(mb_p1_hi)`] for Aur-P1 and [`r n3(mb_p2_lo)`, `r n3(mb_p2_hi)`] for Aur-P2; both span zero. Because the Aur-P2 analysis rests on only `r nrow(aurp2_unique_data)` sites (`r n_pairs_p2` site pairs) and Aur-P1 on `r nrow(aurp1_unique_data)` sites (`r n_pairs_p1` pairs), the Mantel test has low statistical power: the wide intervals mean a true moderate geographic correlation (|r| ≈ 0.3–0.4) would fall well inside the sampling noise and could not be excluded. The non-significant Mantel result must therefore be read as a *lack of evidence* for geographic structure, not as evidence that geographic structure is absent, and (consistent with S5.10) it provides no support for any alternative cultural process.

## S5.12 Time-Series Style Check: Does Sign Dissimilarity Increase with Temporal Lag? {#sec-s5-12}

### Rationale

The main text reports a temporal Mantel test in which sign dissimilarity is correlated with temporal distance (|ΔMedianBP|); that test is weakly but nominally significant (R ≈ 0.06, p ≈ 0.004) yet explains little variation, and the reviewer correctly notes it cannot demonstrate whether substantial change in sign types did or did not occur through time. A single global Mantel R is also indirect: it asks whether time and composition co-vary on average, not whether sites *further apart in time* have *more dissimilar* repertoires. To test temporal turnover more directly we ask three specific questions:

1. **Does sign dissimilarity increase with temporal lag?** We bin all site pairs by their absolute temporal separation (|ΔMedianBP|) and ask whether mean Jaccard dissimilarity of sign presence/absence rises as the lag grows — the signature of gradual compositional change through time.
2. **Is any time signal driven by the between-phase gap or by gradual within-phase change?** Because the two-phase scheme pools spans of several millennia, most temporal variance in a pooled sample is the ~5 ka gap between Aur-P1 and Aur-P2. We therefore separate within-phase pairs (gradual change) from between-phase pairs (the phase boundary) and test the lag–dissimilarity trend in each.
3. **How should a flat or null trend be interpreted?** We state explicitly whether a non-significant result establishes absence of change, or merely a lack of evidence, given the small sample and time-averaging.

### Analysis

We aggregate the cleaned object-level data to **site level**: for each of the `r n_sites_ts` sites we record the presence/absence of every sign type (any object at the site carrying the sign counts as present) and a single calibrated age taken as the median `MedianBP` (years BP) across the site's objects. Pairwise Jaccard dissimilarity of the binary sign vectors and the absolute temporal lag |ΔMedianBP| (converted to ka) are computed for all `r n_pairs_ts` unordered site pairs. The lag–dissimilarity trend is tested with Spearman rank correlation, overall and restricted to within-phase pairs, and summarised in temporal-lag bins.

```{r}
#| label: s5-12-time-lag
#| warning: false

# Site-level time-lag check, computed once in functions.R (time_lag_pairs).
tl <- time_lag_pairs(signbase_full_clean)
n_sites_ts       <- tl$n_sites
n_p1_ts          <- tl$n_p1
n_p2_ts          <- tl$n_p2
n_pairs_ts       <- tl$n_pairs
ts_rho_all       <- tl$rho_all
ts_p_all         <- tl$p_all
ts_rho_within    <- tl$rho_within
ts_p_within      <- tl$p_within
mean_jac_within  <- tl$mean_jac_within
mean_jac_between <- tl$mean_jac_between
mean_lag_within  <- tl$mean_lag_within
mean_lag_between <- tl$mean_lag_between
ts_bin_tab       <- tl$bin_tab
ts_jac_short     <- tl$jac_short
ts_last_bin      <- tl$last_bin
ts_last_n        <- tl$last_n
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ts-lag
#| tbl-cap: "Mean Jaccard dissimilarity of geometric-sign repertoires by temporal-lag class (absolute |ΔMedianBP| between site pairs, in ka). Each row pools all site pairs whose temporal separation falls in the bin; Pairs is the number of site pairs; Mean Jaccard dissimilarity is the average over those pairs."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom

kable(ts_bin_tab, digits = 3)
```

### Interpretation

**Question 1 — does sign dissimilarity increase with temporal lag?** No. Across all `r n_pairs_ts` site pairs the Spearman correlation between temporal lag (|ΔMedianBP|, ka) and Jaccard sign dissimilarity is `r ts_rho_all` (p = `r ts_p_all`) — essentially zero and non-significant — so dissimilarity does not rise as sites become more separated in time. The binned means are flat and non-monotonic (@tbl-ts-lag): mean dissimilarity is `r ts_jac_short` at the shortest lags (0–2 ka) and shows no orderly increase at longer lags; the highest-lag bin (`r ts_last_bin`, only `r ts_last_n` pairs) is too sparsely sampled to support any trend. As a more direct test of temporal turnover than the single global temporal Mantel, this analysis finds no evidence that sign repertoires became more dissimilar with time.

**Question 2 — is any time signal driven by the between-phase gap or by gradual within-phase change?** The time signal is absent in both components. Within-phase pairs (mean lag `r mean_lag_within` ka) give ρ = `r ts_rho_within` (p = `r ts_p_within`), again flat. The between-phase gap dominates the temporal variance of the pooled sample — between-phase pairs have a mean lag of `r mean_lag_between` ka, roughly double the within-phase mean — yet between-phase pairs are if anything slightly *less* dissimilar (mean Jaccard `r mean_jac_between`) than within-phase pairs (mean Jaccard `r mean_jac_within`). The ~5 ka phase boundary therefore does not impose a temporal-turnover signal: sites in different phases are no more dissimilar in sign repertoire than sites within the same phase. This also clarifies the main-text temporal Mantel, which was weakly but nominally significant (R ≈ 0.06, p ≈ 0.004) only because it pairs 438 objects that largely share a site `MedianBP`, inflating the effective sample; at the site level, where each age is measured once, no monotonic time trend remains.

**Question 3 — how should a flat trend be interpreted?** A null result here cannot establish that substantial change did *not* occur. The test is underpowered — only `r n_sites_ts` sites (`r n_p1_ts` in Aur-P1, `r n_p2_ts` in Aur-P2) yielding `r n_pairs_ts` pairs — each phase spans several millennia and each site is collapsed to a single `MedianBP` with large calibrated errors (time-averaging), and genuine change could be non-monotonic (signs appearing and later disappearing) or additive (later sites retaining earlier repertoires while adding new ones), either of which would leave Jaccard dissimilarity nearly constant. The lag analysis therefore shows only that the data contain *no strong evidence* of time-structured change in sign repertoires; it does **not** demonstrate the absence of change. This is consistent with the corrected temporal-Mantel wording in the main text and with the S5.10 multiple regression, both of which conclude that temporal distance explains little of the variation in sign composition and cannot establish whether substantial change did or did not occur.

# S6. Robustness of the Two-Group Structure: Bootstrap Consensus and Stochastic Block Models {#sec-s6}

## S6.1 Rationale {#sec-s6-1}

The main-text claim that each phase resolves into two cultural groups, restricted-range versus broader-range sign repertoires, rests on a single Brower-Kile seriation run followed by manual block assignment (see S5). Two limitations remain unaddressed by S1–S5. First, the seriation is a deterministic operation on a single observed sample: no quantity is attached to the *sampling uncertainty* of the resulting block structure, so we do not know whether the same two groups would emerge if sites were resampled. Second, group membership is treated as a hard, analyst-assigned label rather than a probabilistic quantity, so borderline sites (e.g. Les Cottés, Trou al'Wesse, Grotte de la Verpillière I) are forced into a single group without an associated measure of confidence.

This section addresses both limitations. In S6.2 we use bootstrap resampling of sites within each phase to build a **consensus co-clustering matrix** [@Monti_2003], quantifying the stability of the two-group partition as a whole and of each site's assignment. In S6.3 we fit **stochastic block models (SBM)**, which treat block membership as a latent variable, select the number of blocks via the Integrated Classification Likelihood (ICL), and return posterior membership probabilities for every site. In S6.4 we cross-validate the bootstrap and SBM assignments against the main-text restricted/broad groups using the Adjusted Rand Index (ARI).

## S6.2 Bootstrap Consensus Analysis {#sec-s6-2}

### Rationale

For each phase we resample the site-by-sign presence/absence matrix **with replacement** (n = 1000 replicates), recompute Jaccard dissimilarity, and partition the resampled sites into two clusters by Ward-linkage hierarchical clustering on the Jaccard distance. For every pair of original sites we record the proportion of replicates in which the two fall in the same cluster , the *consensus co-clustering probability*. If the two-group structure identified in the main text is genuine, mean co-clustering *within* each block (restricted/broad) should substantially exceed mean co-clustering *across* the two blocks, and sites central to a block should show high per-site consistency (the proportion of replicates in which the site is assigned to its modal block). Low within-block co-clustering identifies sites whose group assignment is not robust to sampling.

```{r}
#| label: s6-boot-functions
# Bootstrap consensus co-clustering into k blocks, from a site x sign matrix.
s6_boot_consensus <- function(mat, n_boot = 1000, k = 2) {
  x <- as.matrix(mat); x[x > 0] <- 1
  sites <- rownames(x); n <- nrow(x)
  co <- matrix(0, n, n, dimnames = list(sites, sites))
  cnt <- matrix(0, n, n, dimnames = list(sites, sites))
  assign <- matrix(0L, n, n_boot, dimnames = list(sites, NULL))
  for (bk in seq_len(n_boot)) {
    set.seed(bk)
    idx <- sample(n, replace = TRUE)
    b <- x[idx, , drop = FALSE]; rownames(b) <- paste0("r", seq_len(n))
    cl <- cutree(hclust(vegan::vegdist(b, "jaccard", binary = TRUE), method = "ward.D2"), k = k)
    for (r in seq_len(n)) assign[idx[r], bk] <- cl[r]
  }
  present <- assign > 0
  for (i in seq_len(n)) for (j in seq_len(n)) if (i < j) {
    v <- present[i, ] & present[j, ]
    cnt[i, j] <- cnt[j, i] <- sum(v)
    if (cnt[i, j] > 0) co[i, j] <- co[j, i] <- sum(assign[i, v] == assign[j, v]) / cnt[i, j]
  }
  # Reference partition obtained by clustering the label-independent consensus
  # matrix; each resample's cluster labels are realigned to this reference to
  # undo the arbitrary label permutation introduced by hierarchical clustering.
  ref <- cutree(hclust(as.dist(1 - co), method = "ward.D2"), k = k)
  names(ref) <- sites
  for (bk in seq_len(n_boot)) {
    idx <- which(present[, bk]); a <- assign[idx, bk]
    agree_id <- sum((a == 1) == (ref[idx] == 1))
    agree_sw <- sum((a == 1) == (ref[idx] == 2))
    if (agree_sw > agree_id) a <- ifelse(a == 1, 2, 1)
    assign[idx, bk] <- a
  }
  modal <- apply(assign, 1, function(v) { t <- table(v[v > 0]); as.integer(names(t)[which.max(t)]) })
  consistency <- vapply(seq_len(n), function(i) {
    v <- assign[i, ]; v <- v[v > 0]
    if (!length(v)) NA_real_ else mean(v == modal[i])
  }, numeric(1))
  names(consistency) <- sites
  list(consensus = co, partition = ref, modal = modal, consistency = consistency)
}
```

```{r}
#| label: s6-boot-compute
# Main-text restricted(1)/broad(2) groups for the two-phase framework (from functions.R).
s6_groups <- manual_groups

s6_art <- list(aurp1_artifact_data, aurp2_artifact_data)
names(s6_art) <- names(s6_groups)
set.seed(42)
s6_boot <- lapply(s6_art, s6_boot_consensus, n_boot = 1000)

tri <- function(m) m[upper.tri(m)]
s6_summary <- map_dfr(names(s6_boot), function(ph) {
  cs  <- s6_boot[[ph]]$consensus
  sit <- rownames(cs)
  g   <- s6_groups[[ph]][sit]
  wr  <- mean(tri(cs[sit[g == 1], sit[g == 1]]), na.rm = TRUE)
  wb  <- mean(tri(cs[sit[g == 2], sit[g == 2]]), na.rm = TRUE)
  xr  <- mean(cs[sit[g == 1], sit[g == 2]], na.rm = TRUE)
  nr  <- sum(g == 1); nb <- sum(g == 2)
  ov  <- (choose(nr, 2) * wr + choose(nb, 2) * wb) / (choose(nr, 2) + choose(nb, 2))
  data.frame(Phase = ph, Restricted_n = nr, Broad_n = nb,
             Within_restricted = round(wr, 2), Within_broad = round(wb, 2),
             Overall_within = round(ov, 2), Across = round(xr, 2),
             stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
})

s6_site_tab <- map_dfr(names(s6_boot), function(ph) {
  cs <- s6_boot[[ph]]
  data.frame(Phase = ph,
             Site = names(cs$consistency),
             Modal_block = cs$modal,
             Consistency = round(cs$consistency, 2),
             stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
})
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-bootstrap-summary
#| tbl-cap: "Bootstrap consensus co-clustering within and across the main-text restricted/broad blocks, by phase (n = 1000 resamples). Within-restricted and Within-broad are the mean co-clustering probabilities among site pairs belonging to the same main-text block; Across is the mean co-clustering probability for pairs in different blocks. If the two-group structure is genuine, within-block values should substantially exceed the across-block value."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom

kable(s6_summary,
      col.names = c("Phase", "Restricted n", "Broad n", "Within restricted",
                    "Within broad", "Overall within", "Across"),
      digits = 2, align = "lcccccc")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-bootstrap-sites
#| tbl-cap: "Per-site bootstrap consistency: proportion of 1000 resamples in which each site is assigned to its modal (most frequent) block. Consistency near 1 indicates robust assignment; values near 0.5 indicate sites whose group membership flips across resamples."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom

kable(s6_site_tab,
      col.names = c("Phase", "Site", "Modal block", "Consistency"),
      digits = 2, align = "llcc")
```

```{r fig.height=10, fig.width=9}
#| label: fig-bootstrap-consensus
#| fig-cap: "Consensus co-clustering matrices from 1000 bootstrap resamples of sites within each phase. Cell colour encodes the probability that two sites fall in the same cluster across resamples (1 = always together, 0 = never). Rows and columns are ordered by hierarchical clustering of the consensus matrix. Strong diagonal blocks indicate sites that reliably co-cluster; pale blocks indicate fuzzy, sampling-dependent membership."
#| fig-width: 8

s6_heatmap <- function(ph) {
  cs <- s6_boot[[ph]]$consensus
  hc <- hclust(as.dist(1 - cs), method = "ward.D2")
  ord <- hc$labels[hc$order]
  long <- cs[ord, ord] %>%
    as.data.frame() %>%
    tibble::rownames_to_column("site1") %>%
    pivot_longer(-site1, names_to = "site2", values_to = "p") %>%
    mutate(site1 = factor(site1, levels = rev(ord)),
           site2 = factor(site2, levels = ord))
  ggplot(long, aes(site2, site1, fill = p)) +
    geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.3) +
    scale_fill_gradient(low = "#FFFFFF", high = "#1F77B4", limits = c(0, 1),
                        name = "Co-clustering") +
    labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
          legend.key.height = unit(0.9, "cm"),
          panel.grid = element_blank())
}

s6_heatmaps <- cowplot::plot_grid(
  plotlist = lapply(names(s6_boot), function(ph)
    s6_heatmap(ph) + ggtitle(ph)),
  ncol = 1, labels = c("a", "b"), label_size = 14)

ggsave(here::here("figures/bootstrap-consensus-plot.png"),
       s6_heatmaps, width = 9, height = 10, bg = "white")

knitr::include_graphics(here::here("figures/bootstrap-consensus-plot.png"))
```

### Interpretation

The bootstrap consensus analysis supports the main-text two-group partition as a **coherent, non-random division of the sign data** in each phase, while quantifying how much tighter one block is than the other. In **Aur-P1**, mean within-block co-clustering is `r s6_summary$Within_restricted[s6_summary$Phase == "Aur-P1"]` for the restricted-range block and `r s6_summary$Within_broad[s6_summary$Phase == "Aur-P1"]` for the broader-range block, against `r s6_summary$Across[s6_summary$Phase == "Aur-P1"]` across the two blocks , a strong signal that both groups are internally coherent and sharply separated. In **Aur-P2**, the pattern is `r s6_summary$Within_restricted[s6_summary$Phase == "Aur-P2"]` within the restricted block and `r s6_summary$Within_broad[s6_summary$Phase == "Aur-P2"]` within the broader block, against `r s6_summary$Across[s6_summary$Phase == "Aur-P2"]` across the blocks.

**Per-site stability.** The site-level consistency values (@tbl-bootstrap-sites) show that the strength of the two-group structure is not uniform across sites. Most sites are placed with their modal block in more than 80% of resamples, but a small number are systematically unstable. The least stable sites are the small, low-richness assemblages whose assignment flips across resamples; per-site consistency values in @tbl-bootstrap-sites identify the sites whose block assignment should be read as provisional in the main text. For the reader, the consensus matrices in @fig-bootstrap-consensus provide a direct visual measure of where the two-block structure is tight (dark blocks) and where it dissolves (pale blocks).

**Implications for the main text.** The two-group structure does not dissolve under resampling: within-block co-clustering exceeds across-block co-clustering in both phases, so the broad qualitative claim of a persistent restricted/broad divide is robust to sampling variation. However, the analysis also qualifies the claim: the *strength* of each group differs by phase (and Aur-P2 is far smaller than Aur-P1), and a minority of sites have genuinely ambiguous membership. The main text should therefore present the two groups as a robust but not invariant partition, with per-site confidence available in @tbl-bootstrap-sites.

## S6.3 Stochastic Block Models {#sec-s6-3}

### Rationale

The bootstrap treats block structure as a resampling artefact of an observed partition. The stochastic block model (SBM) takes a different route: it treats block membership as an unobserved latent variable and asks which *generative* model of network structure best explains the observed pattern of sign sharing. In the SBM, the probability that two sites are connected depends only on their block memberships. We fit the *symmetric* stochastic block model (`SBM_sym`) using the *weighted* Jaccard similarity adjacency matrix (threshold = 0.2), preserving edge strength rather than binarizing. This is appropriate because Jaccard similarity is symmetric and cultural connectivity is mutual. Fitting the model returns (i) the number of blocks that best fits the data, chosen by the Integrated Classification Likelihood (ICL; a penalised likelihood that trades fit against model complexity), and (ii) the posterior probability of membership in each block for every site. Because ICL is a model-selection criterion, the SBM provides a statistical answer to "how many groups are there?" rather than the visual answer provided by seriation.

```{r}
#| label: s6-sbm-compute
# Fit stochastic block models for both phases (requires `blockmodels` package).
# This runs at render time for full reproducibility; no cached RDS is used.
s6_sbm <- s6_fit_sbm_all(
  list("Aur-P1" = aurp1_artifact_data, "Aur-P2" = aurp2_artifact_data),
  max_K = 5,
  save_path = NULL  # do not cache; compute fresh each render
)
# ── Inline-accessor helpers for the S6.3/S6.4 interpretation text ────────────
# Direct calls to canonical functions in functions.R with local S6 objects.
# These are simple aliases to avoid rewriting inline code.
s6_bestK_wrap   <- function(ph) s6_bestK(s6_sbm, ph)
s6_gap_wrap     <- function(ph) s6_gap(s6_sbm, ph)
s6_global_minPost <- s6_global_minPost(s6_sbm)
s6_mismatch_wrap <- function(ph) s6_mismatch(s6_sbm, s6_boot, s6_groups, ph)
s6_minPost <- function(ph) if (ph %in% names(s6_sbm)) min(apply(s6_sbm[[ph]]$Z, 1, max)) else NA_real_
s6_maxICL  <- function(ph) if (ph %in% names(s6_sbm)) max(s6_sbm[[ph]]$icl, na.rm = TRUE) else NA_real_
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sbm-icl
#| tbl-cap: "Integrated Classification Likelihood (ICL) for stochastic block models with K = 1 to 5 blocks, by phase. The best-supported number of blocks (maximum ICL) is bolded. A decisive maximum (large gap in ICL) indicates that the number of groups is well determined by the data; a flat ICL profile indicates the number of groups is weakly constrained."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom

if (length(s6_sbm)) {
  maxK <- max(vapply(s6_sbm, function(z) length(z$icl), integer(1)))
  icl_tab <- map_dfr(names(s6_sbm), function(ph) {
    z <- s6_sbm[[ph]]
    data.frame(Phase = ph, K = seq_along(z$icl), ICL = round(z$icl, 1))
  }) %>%
    filter(K <= maxK) %>%
    pivot_wider(names_from = K, values_from = ICL, names_prefix = "K = ")
  best_ks <- sapply(s6_sbm, function(z) z$bestK)
  icl_tab$`Best K` <- NA_real_
  for (ph in names(best_ks)) {
    icl_tab$`Best K`[icl_tab$Phase == ph] <- best_ks[[ph]]
  }
  kable(icl_tab, col.names = c("Phase", paste0("K = ", seq_len(maxK)), "Best K"),
        digits = 1, align = "lcccccc")
} else {
  cat("S6.3 requires the `blockmodels` package. Run `renv::install(\"blockmodels\")` and re-render.")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sbm-membership
#| tbl-cap: "Posterior block-membership probabilities and modal (hard) assignment from the best-fitting stochastic block model for each phase. Probabilities are rounded; the modal block is the column with the highest probability. Sites with probability spread across blocks (e.g. no entry above 0.7) have ambiguous membership."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom

if (length(s6_sbm)) {
  s6_mem_tab <- map_dfr(names(s6_sbm), function(ph) {
    z <- s6_sbm[[ph]]
    m <- as.data.frame(z$Z)
    m$Site <- rownames(z$Z)
    m$Phase <- ph
    m$Modal <- apply(z$Z, 1, which.max)
    m %>% dplyr::select(Phase, Site, Modal, everything())
  })
  kable(s6_mem_tab,
        col.names = c("Phase", "Site", "Modal block",
                      paste0("P(", gsub("Block", "B", names(s6_mem_tab)[4:(ncol(s6_mem_tab))]), ")")),
        digits = 2, align = "llc")
} else {
  cat("S6.3 requires the `blockmodels` package. Run `renv::install(\"blockmodels\")` and re-render.")
}
```

### Interpretation

The ICL model-selection results (@tbl-sbm-icl) report the number of blocks best supported by the sign-sharing network in each phase, providing a model-based counterpart to the seriation. The Integrated Classification Likelihood (ICL) is a penalised likelihood criterion that balances model fit against complexity; unlike AIC or BIC, it integrates over the latent block memberships and therefore directly targets the quality of the partition itself. In **Aur-P1** the best-supported model contains `r s6_bestK_wrap("Aur-P1")` block (ICL = `r n2(s6_maxICL("Aur-P1"))`), while the two-block solution scores `r n2(s6_sbm[["Aur-P1"]]$icl[2])` and the three-block solution `r n2(s6_sbm[["Aur-P1"]]$icl[3])`. The ICL gap between the best and second-best model is `r n2(s6_gap_wrap("Aur-P1"))`, indicating that the one-block model is preferred but the preference is modest—the data do not strongly discriminate among one, two, or three blocks. In **Aur-P2** the ICL profile is similarly flat: the one-block model scores `r n2(s6_sbm[["Aur-P2"]]$icl[1])`, the two-block model `r n2(s6_sbm[["Aur-P2"]]$icl[2])`, and the gap is only `r n2(s6_gap_wrap("Aur-P2"))`. In both phases the sparse sign-sharing networks (Aur-P1: 20 sites, `r nrow(aurp1_artifact_data)` edges at threshold 0.2; Aur-P2: 9 sites, `r nrow(aurp2_artifact_data)` edges) lack the information to decisively support any block structure beyond a single group. The comparison between the two phases shows that neither phase has a well-determined block structure under the generative SBM framework.

The membership table (@tbl-sbm-membership) gives posterior probabilities that qualify the deterministic group assignments used in the main text. The SBM treats block membership as a latent variable and estimates, for each site, a probability distribution over blocks; the modal block is the one with highest posterior probability. With a single block selected in both phases, every site is assigned to that sole block with posterior probability 1.0. The informative quantity is therefore not the partition (which is trivial) but the fact that the generative model finds no evidence for multiple blocks in either phase. The model-based route neither corroborates nor contradicts the manual two-group split—it simply indicates that the sign-sharing networks are too sparse to resolve block structure.

Where the number of blocks matches the seriation's two-group structure and posterior probabilities are high, the two-group claim would be independently corroborated by a generative model that was never shown the seriation solution. Here, the SBM favours a single block in both phases, meaning it does not recover the two-group partition. This does not imply the two groups are absent; rather, the SBM's generative framework—with its penalty for model complexity via ICL—requires stronger evidence for multiple blocks than the data provide. The manual restricted/broad assignment, defined partly by sign-type *richness* rather than purely by compositional *similarity*, may capture a real contrast (rich vs. poor sign repertoires) that is not well modelled as a block structure in the sign-sharing network.

The SBM results must be interpreted alongside the bootstrap consensus (S6.2) and Louvain community detection (S5.1), as each method answers a different question. The bootstrap quantifies *sampling stability* of the observed two-group partition: it asks whether the same partition would emerge from slightly different samples of sites, and finds that within-block co-clustering exceeds across-block co-clustering in both phases, confirming the partition is not an artefact of a particular site sample. Louvain community detection (S5.1) is a descriptive modularity-optimisation algorithm that partitions the observed network without a generative model; it identifies `r s51_ncomm$ncomm[s51_ncomm$Phase == "Aur-P1" & s51_ncomm$Threshold == 0.2]` communities in Aur-P1 at threshold 0.2, with the two largest corresponding closely to the manual restricted/broad split and additional sub-communities within the broader-range group. The SBM is a *generative* model: it posits that edges are generated by latent block memberships and uses ICL to select the number of blocks that best explains the network. The three methods diverge in their conclusions: the bootstrap supports the two-group partition's internal coherence; Louvain detects multiple communities including substructure within the broader-range sites; the SBM selects a single block in both phases. This divergence reflects their different objectives: the bootstrap tests stability of an *imposed* partition; Louvain finds *any* modular structure in the observed network; the SBM asks whether a *generative* block model is warranted by the data, and concludes it is not.

**Implications for the main text.** The SBM selects a single block in both phases, so the two-group structure is not independently recovered by the generative model. The restricted/broad dichotomy should be read as the *dominant axis of variation* (rich vs. poor sign repertoires) rather than a partition that emerges from compositional similarity through an unsupervised generative model. The main findings are therefore: (1)  the two-group framing is a simplification that captures the primary contrast in sign repertoire size, (2) the generative SBM—unlike the descriptive Louvain and stability-based bootstrap—does not find evidence for multiple blocks in either phase, likely due to network sparsity and the ICL penalty for model complexity, (3) the Aur-P2 results are qualified by the small sample size (9 sites, sparse edges) precludes reliable block detection. These results complement the bootstrap analysis: the bootstrap shows the two blocks to be internally coherent and well separated under resampling, while the SBM asks whether an independent generative model reproduces the two-block partition—and finds that the data are too sparse to warrant a multi-block generative model in either phase.

## S6.4 Cross-Validation of Group Assignments (ARI) {#sec-s6-4}

### Rationale

To quantify overall agreement among the three ways of partitioning sites , the main-text manual restricted/broad groups, the bootstrap modal blocks (S6.2), and the SBM modal assignments (S6.3), we compute the Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) between each pair of partitions for each phase. ARI = 1 indicates identical partitions, 0 indicates agreement no better than chance. We use a self-contained implementation of ARI (the S5 analyses use `mclust::adjustedRandIndex`, which yields the same values).

```{r}
#| label: s6-ari
s6_ari <- function(a, b) {
  a <- as.integer(a); b <- as.integer(b)
  n <- length(a)
  tab <- table(a, b)
  ni <- rowSums(tab); nj <- colSums(tab)
  comb2 <- function(x) sum(choose(x, 2))
  N <- sum(tab)
  (sum(choose(as.vector(tab), 2)) - (comb2(ni) * comb2(nj)) / choose(N, 2)) /
    (0.5 * (comb2(ni) + comb2(nj)) - (comb2(ni) * comb2(nj)) / choose(N, 2))
}

s6_ari_tab <- map_dfr(names(s6_boot), function(ph) {
  sit <- names(s6_boot[[ph]]$consistency)
  manual <- s6_groups[[ph]][sit]
  boot_m <- s6_boot[[ph]]$modal[names(manual)]
  # SBM modal assignments: intersect site names to handle any missing sites
  sbm_m <- NULL
  if (length(s6_sbm) && ph %in% names(s6_sbm)) {
    sbm_sites <- rownames(s6_sbm[[ph]]$Z)
    common_sites <- intersect(sit, sbm_sites)
    if (length(common_sites) >= 2) {
      sbm_m <- apply(s6_sbm[[ph]]$Z[common_sites, , drop = FALSE], 1, which.max)
      # Align manual and boot_m to common sites for ARI comparison
      manual <- manual[common_sites]
      boot_m <- boot_m[common_sites]
    }
  }
  row <- data.frame(Phase = ph,
                    ARI_manual_boot  = round(s6_ari(manual, boot_m), 2))
  if (!is.null(sbm_m)) {
    row$ARI_manual_sbm  <- round(s6_ari(manual, sbm_m), 2)
    row$ARI_boot_sbm    <- round(s6_ari(boot_m, sbm_m), 2)
  } else {
    row$ARI_manual_sbm <- NA; row$ARI_boot_sbm <- NA
  }
  row
})

# Cell lookup for the ARI table, e.g. s6_ari_val("Evolved Aurignacian", "ARI_manual_sbm").
s6_ari_val <- function(ph, col) s6_ari_tab[[col]][s6_ari_tab$Phase == ph]
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-s6-ari
#| tbl-cap: "Adjusted Rand Index between the main-text manual restricted/broad assignment, the bootstrap modal blocks (S6.2), and the SBM modal assignments (S6.3), by phase. "
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom

kable(s6_ari_tab,
      col.names = c("Phase", "ARI manual vs bootstrap", "ARI manual vs SBM", "ARI bootstrap vs SBM"),
      digits = 2, align = "lccc")
```

### Interpretation

The ARI values summarise how far the three routes to the two-group partition agree, and the agreement is informative precisely because it varies by phase and method (@tbl-s6-ari). A high ARI between the manual groups and an unsupervised partition (SBM or bootstrap) indicates that the main-text grouping is broadly reproduced by data-driven partitions; because those partitions are also derived from the same sign data, this agreement is not independent confirmation that the groups differ. A low ARI indicates a genuine divergence: the manual restricted/broad split and the partition recovered by an unsupervised method organise the sites differently. Because the restricted/broad divide is defined partly by sign-type *richness* (the restricted sites are assemblages with few sign types), it is not in general expected to coincide with clusters defined purely by compositional *similarity*, and low ARI between the manual groups and similarity-based partitions should be interpreted in that light rather than as evidence that either partition is wrong.  

**Implications for the main text.** The ARI between the manual restricted/broad assignment and the bootstrap modal blocks is `r s6_ari_val("Aur-P1","ARI_manual_boot")` in Aur-P1 and `r s6_ari_val("Aur-P2","ARI_manual_boot")` in Aur-P2 (@tbl-s6-ari). In Aur-P1 this means the bootstrap recovers the manual two-group partition exactly: the main-text claim that Aur-P1 resolves into restricted-range and broader-range sign-repertoire groups is robustly supported and is not an artefact of the particular site sample. In Aur-P2 the value of `r s6_ari_val("Aur-P2","ARI_manual_boot")` means the bootstrap recovers the manual partition only weakly, so the main-text Aur-P2 two-group claim rests on a markedly weaker evidence base than the Aur-P1 claim and is best treated as a provisional pattern. The SBM columns are undefined because the stochastic block model selects a single block in both phases (S6.3); the SBM therefore provides no two-group ARI, and its result that the sign-sharing networks are too sparse to support more than one block is consistent with the bootstrap finding that the Aur-P2 partition is the less robust of the two. These agreements are among partitions derived from the same sign data, so they establish the *recovery and stability* of the two-group structure rather than independent confirmation that the groups differ — that question is addressed in @sec-s6-6.

## S6.5 Summary of Implications {#sec-s6-5}

Taken together, S6 provides three converging but graded lines of evidence for the main-text two-group claim. (1) **Resampling stability**: within-block co-clustering exceeds across-block co-clustering in every phase (@fig-bootstrap-consensus, @tbl-bootstrap-summary), so the partition does not arise from a particular sample of sites. (2) **Model selection**: the SBM attaches posterior probabilities to each site's membership (@tbl-sbm-membership) and reports the number of blocks best supported by the sign-sharing network in each phase (@tbl-sbm-icl). The SBM selects a single block in both Aur-P1 and Aur-P2, indicating that the sparse sign-sharing networks do not provide sufficient evidence for a multi-block generative model—this is a null result for block structure, not a contradiction of the two-group contrast. (3) **Cross-validation**: ARI between the manual, bootstrap, and SBM partitions quantifies their agreement (@tbl-s6-ari). The three routes are mutually informative but not redundant: the bootstrap shows the two blocks to be internally coherent and well separated under resampling; the SBM finds the data too sparse to warrant a multi-block generative model; and the manual assignment captures the dominant axis of variation in sign repertoire size. The circularity of the main-text PerMANOVA itself is addressed separately in @sec-s6-6, which validates the grouping on withheld data rather than on the data used to define it.

# S6.6 Circularity-Breaking Validation of the Restricted/Broad Group Difference {#sec-s6-6}

## Rationale

The restricted/broad groups were defined from the same sign-composition data that the main-text PerMANOVA later tests, so its p-values cannot be read as *independent* confirmation that the groups differ. Louvain, bootstrap and stochastic block model analyses (S5, S6) also operate on that same underlying dataset, so they do not remove the circularity either. To address this directly we implement three complementary methods that break the circularity, each following a distinct validation strategy:

- **(A) Maximally-selected achieved-significance test:** the optimal two-group split is re-derived from *randomised* data in every permutation, and the observed optimal split is compared against that null. This controls for the fact that the grouping was itself optimised to maximise separation.
- **(B) Cross-validation on withheld data:** the grouping is validated on data that did not contribute to its definition. We do this at two levels — (i) site level: leave-one-site-out k-nearest-neighbour classification, where each held-out site is predicted from the other sites only; and (ii) object level: the two-group rule is learned from one random half of each site's objects and tested, by PerMANOVA, on the *other* half.
- **(C) Group-free gradient PerMANOVA:** instead of asserting discrete groups, sign composition is regressed on a continuous ordination axis, testing for a gradient rather than a partition.

All three are exploratory companions to, not replacements for, the main-text PerMANOVA, which we present as descriptive rather than confirmatory.

```{r}
# ── S6.6 computation: circularity-breaking validation ────────────────────────
# Align manual group labels to the site x sign artifact matrices (rownames = sites).
aurp1_grp <- aurp1_unique_data$group[match(rownames(aurp1_artifact_data),
                                           aurp1_unique_data$site_name)]
aurp2_grp <- aurp2_unique_data$group[match(rownames(aurp2_artifact_data),
                                           aurp2_unique_data$site_name)]

sign_cols_all <- intersect(colnames(aurp1_artifact_data), colnames(aurp2_artifact_data))

# (A) Maximally-selected achieved-significance test
s6_6_bestP1 <- best_split_permtest(aurp1_artifact_data, group = aurp1_grp, B = 999, seed = 1)
s6_6_bestP2 <- best_split_permtest(aurp2_artifact_data, group = aurp2_grp, B = 999, seed = 1)

# (B-i) Site-level leave-one-out cross-validated group recovery
s6_6_cvP1 <- cv_group_accuracy(aurp1_artifact_data, aurp1_grp, k = 1, B = 999, seed = 1)
s6_6_cvP2 <- cv_group_accuracy(aurp2_artifact_data, aurp2_grp, k = 1, B = 999, seed = 1)

# (B-ii) Object-level holdout: groups from one half of objects, test on the other
s6_6_objP1 <- cv_permanova_objectsplit(
  signbase_full_clean %>% filter(phase2 == "Aur-P1") %>%
    dplyr::select(site_name, all_of(sign_cols_all)),
  sign_cols_all, B_rep = 100, B_perm = 499, seed = 1)
s6_6_objP2 <- cv_permanova_objectsplit(
  signbase_full_clean %>% filter(phase2 == "Aur-P2") %>%
    dplyr::select(site_name, all_of(sign_cols_all)),
  sign_cols_all, B_rep = 100, B_perm = 499, seed = 1)

# (C) Group-free continuous gradient PerMANOVA on the first PCoA axis
s6_6_D1 <- vegdist(aurp1_artifact_data, "jaccard", binary = TRUE)
s6_6_D2 <- vegdist(aurp2_artifact_data, "jaccard", binary = TRUE)
s6_6_gradP1 <- gradient_permanova(s6_6_D1, cmdscale(s6_6_D1, k = 1)[, 1])
s6_6_gradP2 <- gradient_permanova(s6_6_D2, cmdscale(s6_6_D2, k = 1)[, 1])

# Summary table
s6_6_tab <- data.frame(
  Method = c("A: Maximally-selected split (P1)", "A: Maximally-selected split (P2)",
            "B: LOOCV site classification (P1)", "B: LOOCV site classification (P2)",
            "B: Object-half holdout (P1)", "B: Object-half holdout (P2)",
            "C: Gradient PerMANOVA (P1)", "C: Gradient PerMANOVA (P2)"),
  Statistic = c(round(s6_6_bestP1$observed_best_F, 2), round(s6_6_bestP2$observed_best_F, 2),
                paste0(round(s6_6_cvP1$accuracy, 2), " acc"), paste0(round(s6_6_cvP2$accuracy, 2), " acc"),
                paste0(round(s6_6_objP1$prop_significant * 100), "% splits sig"),
                paste0(round(s6_6_objP2$prop_significant * 100), "% splits sig"),
                paste0("R2 = ", s6_6_gradP1$R2), paste0("R2 = ", s6_6_gradP2$R2)),
  `p-value` = c(round(s6_6_bestP1$p_value, 3), round(s6_6_bestP2$p_value, 3),
                round(s6_6_cvP1$p_value, 3), round(s6_6_cvP2$p_value, 3),
                format.pval(s6_6_objP1$combined_p, digits = 3),
                format.pval(s6_6_objP2$combined_p, digits = 3),
                s6_6_gradP1$p, s6_6_gradP2$p))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-s6-6-summary
#| tbl-cap: "Circularity-breaking validation of the restricted/broad group difference. Method A re-derives the optimal two-group split from randomised data in every permutation (observed optimal pseudo-F vs. its null). Method B validates the grouping on withheld data: site-level leave-one-out k-NN classification accuracy (with permutation p-value) and object-level holdout where groups are defined from one random half of each site's objects and tested on the other half (Fisher-combined p across 100 random splits). Method C is a group-free continuous gradient PerMANOVA on the first PCoA axis. A significant result indicates the group structure is recoverable from data not used to define it."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom
kable(s6_6_tab, digits = 3, align = "llc")
```

### Interpretation

The methods below answer one general question, whether the restricted/broad difference is a genuine pattern recoverable from data independent of how the groups were originally defined, through three specific questions, each answered by a different route.

**Question 1 (strategy A):** Is the observed two-group split *stronger* than the best split one would obtain by optimising on randomised data, that is, does the restricted/broad partition survive a null that accounts for the fact that the grouping was itself optimised to maximise separation? Method A re-derives the optimal split by ordering sites on sign-repertoire richness, the same principle underlying the manual restricted/broad distinction, and compares the observed optimum against the null distribution of optima from randomised data.
- *Answer:* No. The observed optimal split is **not** significant (Aur-P1 observed optimal pseudo-F = `r round(s6_6_bestP1$observed_best_F, 2)`, permutation p = `r s6_6_bestP1$p_value`; Aur-P2 observed optimal pseudo-F = `r round(s6_6_bestP2$observed_best_F, 2)`, permutation p = `r s6_6_bestP2$p_value`). This is consistent with, not contradictory to, the conclusions from strategies B and C below: because B and C independently show the contrast is recoverable from withheld data, the non-significance of A is best read as evidence against a *sharp discontinuous partition* rather than against the contrast existing. The restricted/broad contrast is therefore a real, recoverable *gradient/axis of variation*, but it is not a sharp partition that survives the most stringent "optimisation-accounted-for" null.

**Question 2 (strategy B):** Can the group assignment be recovered from data that did **not** contribute to defining it? 
- *Site level (B-i):* Can a held-out site's restricted/broad label be predicted from a classifier trained only on the other sites?
  - *Answer:* Yes. Leave-one-site-out classification recovers the manual label for `r round(s6_6_cvP1$accuracy * 100)`% of Aur-P1 sites (95% CI `r round(s6_6_cvP1$ci_lo, 2)`–`r round(s6_6_cvP1$ci_hi, 2)`, permutation p = `r s6_6_cvP1$p_value`) and `r round(s6_6_cvP2$accuracy * 100)`% of Aur-P2 sites (permutation p = `r s6_6_cvP2$p_value`). A site's group is therefore predictable from a classifier trained on the *other* sites, so the assignment is not an artefact of fitting all sites simultaneously.
- *Object level (B-ii):* When the two-group rule is learned from one random half of each site's objects and tested, by PerMANOVA, on the *other* half, is the held-out contrast still significant?
  - *Answer:* Yes for Aur-P1: the held-out PerMANOVA is significant in the large majority of random splits (`r round(s6_6_objP1$prop_significant * 100)`% of 100; Fisher-combined p = `r format.pval(s6_6_objP1$combined_p, digits=2)`), using `r s6_6_objP1$n_usable` of `r nrow(aurp1_artifact_data)` sites that have enough objects for splitting. For Aur-P2 the combined evidence is likewise significant (Fisher-combined p = `r format.pval(s6_6_objP2$combined_p, digits=2)`), although only `r s6_6_objP2$n_usable` of `r nrow(aurp2_artifact_data)` Aur-P2 sites have two or more objects, so each individual split has low power (few splits clear p < 0.05 on their own) and the conclusion for Aur-P2 rests on the combined test rather than any single split. This shows the grouping is stable across *disjoint sets of objects*, which the original PerMANOVA, using every object to both define and test the groups, could not establish.

**Question 3 (strategy C):** If we abandon the discrete two-group partition entirely and instead ask whether sign composition varies continuously along the main compositional axis, is that gradient significant?
- *Answer:* Yes. A group-free gradient PerMANOVA regressing sign composition on the continuous first ordination axis is significant in both phases (Aur-P1: R² = `r s6_6_gradP1$R2`, p = `r s6_6_gradP1$p`; Aur-P2: R² = `r s6_6_gradP2$R2`, p = `r s6_6_gradP2$p`). Even without asserting discrete groups, a compositional gradient explains a significant fraction of the variation.

**Summary.** Strategies B and C provide the strongest evidence that the
restricted/broad contrast is not a circularity artefact: the grouping is
recovered from withheld data (strategy B) and a continuous gradient is significant without any group definition (strategy C). Strategy A, the most conservative test, is consistent with a gradual rather than sharp partition and does not contradict the recoverability established by B and C. We therefore present the main-text PerMANOVA as descriptive and exploratory, and we rely on the cross-validation results (strategy B) as the appropriate independent confirmation that the grouping is not a circularity artefact.
# S7. Object-Type Sensitivity: Figurine Exclusion {#sec-s7}


```{r}
#| label: s7-setup
#| include: false
# ── S7 setup: all figurine-exclusion statistics are produced by the shared
#    sensitivity_summary() function in functions.R (also used by paper.qmd and the
#    S8 section), so the supplement and the main text cannot report divergent numbers.

excl <- sensitivity_summary(signbase_full_clean, aurp1_artifact_data, aurp2_artifact_data)

figurine_types   <- excl$figurine_types
figurine_summary <- excl$figurine_summary
s7_baseline      <- excl$s7_baseline
s7_no_fig        <- excl$s7_no_fig
s7_no_vog        <- excl$s7_no_vog_fig
s7_sites_lost    <- excl$s7_sites_lost
s7_vog_before    <- excl$s7_vog_before
s7_vog_summary   <- excl$s7_vog_summary
joint_comparison <- excl$joint_comparison

s7_fig_count <- function(site) figurine_summary$Total[figurine_summary$site_name == site]
s7_fig_count_cond <- function(site, ph) {
  sum(figurine_summary$Total[figurine_summary$site_name == site & figurine_summary$phase2 == ph])
}
s7_fig_total <- sum(figurine_summary$Total)
s7_fig_p1 <- sum(figurine_summary$Total[figurine_summary$phase2 == "Aur-P1"])
s7_fig_p2 <- sum(figurine_summary$Total[figurine_summary$phase2 == "Aur-P2"])
```

## S7.1 Rationale

@Bentz_Dutkiewicz_2026 demonstrate that ivory figurines in the Swabian Aurignacian carry sign sequences with higher information density than tools. If figurines encode different sign repertoires than other object types, their inclusion could bias site-level sign assemblages , particularly at Vogelherd, where `r s7_fig_count("Vogelherd")` of the dataset's `r s7_fig_total` figurines are concentrated. This section tests whether the main-text network findings are robust to the exclusion of figurines, both globally and site-specifically.

## S7.2 Figurine Distribution in the Dataset

```{r}
#| label: tbl-figurine-count
#| tbl-cap: "Distribution of figurine objects across phases and sites. Figurine types include figurine zoomorph, figurine anthropomorph, figurine undet., and possible figurine."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom
# figurine_summary is precomputed in the s7-setup chunk

kable(figurine_summary,
      col.names = c("Phase", "Site",
                    grep("figurine", names(figurine_summary), value = TRUE, invert = FALSE),
                    "Total"),
      digits = 0)
```

```{r}
#| label: s7-helpers
#| include: false
# ── Accessor helpers for the S7 interpretation prose (read from joint_comparison) ──
s7_md  <- function(ph, cond = "Baseline (all objects)") {
  round(joint_comparison$mean_degree[joint_comparison$Phase == ph & joint_comparison$Condition == cond], 2)
}
s7_ed  <- function(ph, cond = "Baseline (all objects)") {
  joint_comparison$n_edges[joint_comparison$Phase == ph & joint_comparison$Condition == cond]
}
s7_ns  <- function(ph, cond = "Baseline (all objects)") {
  joint_comparison$n_sites[joint_comparison$Phase == ph & joint_comparison$Condition == cond]
}
s7_mo  <- function(ph, cond = "Baseline (all objects)") {
  round(joint_comparison$modularity[joint_comparison$Phase == ph & joint_comparison$Condition == cond], 3)
}
s7_tr  <- function(ph, cond = "Baseline (all objects)") {
  round(joint_comparison$transitivity[joint_comparison$Phase == ph & joint_comparison$Condition == cond], 3)
}
s7_pct <- function(cond) {
  paste0(round(joint_comparison$pct_change_md[
    joint_comparison$Phase == "Aur-P1" & joint_comparison$Condition == cond], 1), "%")
}
```

@tbl-figurine-count shows that figurines are heavily concentrated at Vogelherd (`r s7_fig_count("Vogelherd")` objects), with minor representation at Hohle Fels (`r s7_fig_count("Hohle Fels")`), Geissenklösterle (`r s7_fig_count("Geissenklösterle")`), Hohlenstein-Stadel (`r s7_fig_count("Hohlenstein-Stadel")`), and La Ferrassie (`r s7_fig_count("La Ferrassie")`). Of these, `r s7_fig_p1` fall within Aur-P1 and the remaining `r s7_fig_p2` , all Hohle Fels objects from AH IV and Iid , fall within Aur-P2 under the layer-level assignment. The analysis therefore tests whether the Aur-P1 network structure , which reports the higher mean degree (`r s7_md("Aur-P1")`) , is driven by these `r s7_fig_count("Vogelherd")` objects at a single site.

## S7.3 Analysis 1: Exclude All Figurines

### Method

We remove all objects where `object_type` contains "figurine" (63 objects total: 25 zoomorph, 10 undetermined, 5 anthropomorph, 23 possible figurine) from the full cleaned dataset, recompute site-level sign matrices by summing remaining objects per site, and rebuild networks at the baseline threshold of 0.2.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-exclude-figurines
#| tbl-cap: "Network statistics before and after excluding all figurine objects (figurine zoomorph, figurine anthropomorph, figurine undet., and possible figurine). Threshold = 0.2, Jaccard similarity."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom
# s7_baseline and s7_no_fig are precomputed in the s7-setup chunk

excl_comparison <- bind_rows(s7_baseline, s7_no_fig)

kable(excl_comparison,
      col.names = c("Phase", "Sites", "Edges", "Density", "Mean degree",
                    "Transitivity", "Modularity", "Condition"),
      digits = 3,
      align = "llcccccc")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-figurine-sites-lost
#| tbl-cap: "Number of sites per phase before and after figurine exclusion. Sites are lost when all objects at that site are figurines."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom

kable(s7_sites_lost %>% dplyr::select(Phase, sites_before, sites_after, lost),
      col.names = c("Phase", "Sites (all)", "Sites (no figurines)", "Sites lost"),
      digits = 0)
```

### Interpretation

Excluding all `r s7_fig_total` figurines has only a small effect on the Aur-P1 network: one edge is lost (`r s7_ed("Aur-P1")` → `r s7_ed("Aur-P1","Exclude all figurines")`) and mean degree falls from `r s7_md("Aur-P1")` to `r s7_md("Aur-P1","Exclude all figurines")`, with no sites lost (all `r s7_ns("Aur-P1")` sites retained). Aur-P2 is unchanged (mean degree `r s7_md("Aur-P2")`, `r s7_ed("Aur-P2")` edges, `r s7_ns("Aur-P2")` sites): the `r s7_fig_count_cond("Hohle Fels","Aur-P2")` Hohle Fels figurines removed from it do not alter the site's sign repertoire, so its network is unaffected. The detectable Aur-P1 effects are declines in transitivity (`r s7_tr("Aur-P1")` → `r s7_tr("Aur-P1","Exclude all figurines")`) and modularity (`r s7_mo("Aur-P1")` → `r s7_mo("Aur-P1","Exclude all figurines")`), indicating that figurines contribute modestly to community cohesion but do not create the communities themselves.

Critically, Aur-P1 retains the higher mean degree (`r s7_md("Aur-P1","Exclude all figurines")`) under figurine exclusion, preserving the main-text ordering Aur-P1 > Aur-P2 (`r s7_md("Aur-P1","Exclude all figurines")` > `r s7_md("Aur-P2")`). The Aur-P1 network remains the more connected regardless of figurine inclusion, confirming that its structure is not contingent on figurine-bearing sign assemblages at Vogelherd.

## S7.4 Analysis 2: Exclude Vogelherd Figurines Only

### Method

Rather than removing all figurines globally, this analysis removes only the 50 figurines from Vogelherd , the site where figurines are most concentrated , while retaining figurines at other sites. This tests whether the Aur-P1 network structure is driven by a single outlier assemblage.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-vogelherd-exclude
#| tbl-cap: "Network statistics before and after excluding figurines from Vogelherd only. All other figurines (Hohle Fels, Geissenklösterle, Hohlenstein-Stadel, La Ferrassie) are retained. Threshold = 0.2, Jaccard similarity."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom
# s7_baseline, s7_no_vog and s7_vog_summary are precomputed in the s7-setup chunk

vog_comparison <- bind_rows(s7_baseline, s7_no_vog)

kable(vog_comparison,
      col.names = c("Phase", "Sites", "Edges", "Density", "Mean degree",
                    "Transitivity", "Modularity", "Condition"),
      digits = 3,
      align = "llcccccc")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-vogelherd-objects
#| tbl-cap: "Vogelherd object counts before and after removing figurines. Non-figurine objects at Vogelherd (tools, plaquettes, etc.) are retained."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom

kable(s7_vog_summary %>% dplyr::select(Phase, objects_before, objects_after, removed),
      col.names = c("Phase", "Objects (all)", "Objects (no figurines)", "Removed"),
      digits = 0)
```

### Interpretation

Removing only Vogelherd's figurines (`r s7_fig_count("Vogelherd")` objects: `r s7_vog_before$objects_before[s7_vog_before$phase2 == "Aur-P1"]` → `r s7_vog_summary$objects_after[s7_vog_summary$Phase == "Aur-P1"]` in Aur-P1) has a negligible effect on Aur-P1: mean degree drops from `r s7_md("Aur-P1")` to `r s7_md("Aur-P1","Exclude Vogelherd figurines")` (`r s7_pct("Exclude Vogelherd figurines")`), one edge is lost (`r s7_ed("Aur-P1")` → `r s7_ed("Aur-P1","Exclude Vogelherd figurines")`), and modularity decreases from `r s7_mo("Aur-P1")` to `r s7_mo("Aur-P1","Exclude Vogelherd figurines")`. Aur-P2 shows no change whatsoever (mean degree `r s7_md("Aur-P2")` → `r s7_md("Aur-P2","Exclude Vogelherd figurines")`, modularity `r s7_mo("Aur-P2")` → `r s7_mo("Aur-P2","Exclude Vogelherd figurines")`), confirming that Vogelherd figurines do not contribute to network structure in the later phase.

The effect of removing Vogelherd figurines alone (`r s7_pct("Exclude Vogelherd figurines")` in Aur-P1) is the same as removing all `r s7_fig_total` figurines globally (`r s7_pct("Exclude all figurines")`), and in both cases the network is essentially unchanged. The figurine effect therefore does not scale with the number of figurines removed; figurines at Hohle Fels (`r s7_fig_count("Hohle Fels")`), Geissenklösterle (`r s7_fig_count("Geissenklösterle")`), Hohlenstein-Stadel (`r s7_fig_count("Hohlenstein-Stadel")`), and La Ferrassie (`r s7_fig_count("La Ferrassie")`) do not alter the network structure , including the `r s7_fig_count_cond("Hohle Fels","Aur-P2")` Hohle Fels figurines assigned to Aur-P2, which leave that phase's network unchanged , and Vogelherd's connectivity within Aur-P1 is carried by its `r s7_vog_summary$objects_after[s7_vog_summary$Phase == "Aur-P1"]` non-figurine objects.

## S7.5 Joint Comparison

```{r}
#| label: tbl-objtype-joint
#| tbl-cap: "Side-by-side comparison of network statistics across all conditions: baseline (all objects), exclude all figurines, and exclude Vogelherd figurines only. The rightmost columns show the percentage change in mean degree from baseline."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom
# joint_comparison is precomputed in the s7-setup chunk

kable(joint_comparison,
      col.names = c("Phase", "Condition", "Sites", "Edges", "Mean degree",
                    "Transitivity", "Modularity", "Δ mean degree (%)"),
      digits = 3,
      align = "lllccccc")
```

## S7.6 Interpretation

The joint comparison in @tbl-objtype-joint shows that figurine exclusion has a modest and phase-dependent effect on network structure:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-s7-6-meandegree
#| tbl-cap: "Mean degree by figurine-exclusion condition, with percentage change from baseline. Reproduced directly from the joint comparison in @tbl-objtype-joint."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom

s7_md_summary <- joint_comparison %>%
  dplyr::select(Phase, Condition, mean_degree, pct_change_md) %>%
  mutate(short = case_when(
    Condition == "Baseline (all objects)"      ~ "Baseline",
    Condition == "Exclude all figurines"       ~ "No figurines",
    Condition == "Exclude Vogelherd figurines" ~ "Vogelherd only")) %>%
  pivot_wider(id_cols = Phase, names_from = short,
              values_from = c(mean_degree, pct_change_md)) %>%
  dplyr::select(
    Phase,
    `Baseline mean degree` = `mean_degree_Baseline`,
    `No figurines`        = `mean_degree_No figurines`,
    delta_no              = `pct_change_md_No figurines`,
    `Vogelherd only`      = `mean_degree_Vogelherd only`,
    delta_vog             = `pct_change_md_Vogelherd only`) %>%
  mutate(
    delta_no  = paste0(formatC(delta_no,  digits = 1, format = "f"), "%"),
    delta_vog = paste0(formatC(delta_vog, digits = 1, format = "f"), "%"))

kable(s7_md_summary,
      col.names = c("Phase", "Baseline mean degree", "No figurines", "Δ",
                    "Vogelherd only", "Δ"),
      digits = c(0, 2, 2, 0, 2, 0),
      align = "llcccc")
```

**Outcome observed: Negligible effect, no qualitative change.** Mean degree changes are at most `r s7_pct("Exclude all figurines")` across both phases and all conditions, and excluding all figurines removes a single edge from Aur-P1 (`r s7_ed("Aur-P1")` → `r s7_ed("Aur-P1","Exclude all figurines")`, mean degree `r s7_md("Aur-P1")` → `r s7_md("Aur-P1","Exclude all figurines")`) while leaving Aur-P2's edge set unchanged (`r s7_ed("Aur-P2")` edges, mean degree `r s7_md("Aur-P2")`). Modularity decreases slightly for Aur-P1 when figurines are excluded (`r s7_mo("Aur-P1")` → `r s7_mo("Aur-P1","Exclude all figurines")` excluding all; `r s7_mo("Aur-P1")` → `r s7_mo("Aur-P1","Exclude Vogelherd figurines")` excluding Vogelherd only) while Aur-P2 is unchanged (`r s7_mo("Aur-P2")`), indicating that figurines contribute marginally to within-group cohesion but do not create the community structure.

**Phase ordering is preserved.** The main-text connectivity contrast Aur-P1 > Aur-P2 (`r s7_md("Aur-P1")` > `r s7_md("Aur-P2")`) is unchanged under both exclusion scenarios (`r s7_md("Aur-P1","Exclude all figurines")` > `r s7_md("Aur-P2")` excluding all figurines; `r s7_md("Aur-P1","Exclude Vogelherd figurines")` > `r s7_md("Aur-P2")` excluding Vogelherd figurines only), preserving the key finding that the early phase is the more connected.

**The figurine effect is small and Vogelherd-specific.** Removing Vogelherd figurines alone (`r s7_pct("Exclude Vogelherd figurines")` in Aur-P1) produces the same effect as removing all `r s7_fig_total` figurines globally (`r s7_pct("Exclude all figurines")`). Figurines at Hohle Fels (`r s7_fig_count("Hohle Fels")`), Geissenklösterle (`r s7_fig_count("Geissenklösterle")`), Hohlenstein-Stadel (`r s7_fig_count("Hohlenstein-Stadel")`), and La Ferrassie (`r s7_fig_count("La Ferrassie")`) do not alter network structure. This indicates that although Vogelherd's figurine assemblage is unusually rich , `r s7_fig_count("Vogelherd")` of `r s7_fig_total` figurines , and contributes disproportionately to sign-type counts, its `r s7_vog_summary$objects_after[s7_vog_summary$Phase == "Aur-P1"]` remaining non-figurine objects still carry a sufficiently diverse sign repertoire to maintain network connectivity.

**Conclusion.** The main-text findings are robust to figurine exclusion. The Aur-P1 > Aur-P2 connectivity contrast, the two-group community structure, and the site membership of both phases are all preserved when figurines are removed. The concentration of figurines at Vogelherd does not bias the seriation or network results, and the broader-range group's connectivity within Aur-P1 is supported by non-figurine sign types. We note that modularity decreases slightly when figurines are excluded (Aur-P1: `r s7_mo("Aur-P1")` → `r s7_mo("Aur-P1","Exclude all figurines")`), suggesting that figurines contribute modestly to community cohesion , consistent with @Bentz_Dutkiewicz_2026 argument that figurines carry high-information sign sequences, but the communities themselves are defined by shared sign types across all object types.

# S8. Site Reclassification Sensitivity Analysis {#sec-s8}

## S8.1 Rationale

The main analysis assigns each site to a phase (Aur-P1/Aur-P2) using specialist technological attributions from the published literature, supplemented by calibrated radiocarbon dates, as detailed in the "Site Phase Assignments" supplementary item. Recent specialist reassessments demonstrate that radiocarbon dates alone are insufficient for phase attribution, and that the archaeological content of layers should take precedence:

- **Abri Pataud**: The lithic technology in levels 14–9 (carinated scraper bladelet cores, dual reduction systems) is diagnostic of the Early Aurignacian (Aur-P1), not the Proto-Aurignacian, despite basal dates of ~41,200–39,500 cal BP that fall within the Proto-Aurignacian range [@Chiotti_2005; @Higham_Abri_Pataud_2011]. The site is classified as Aurignacian I (Early) in the Périgord sequence.
- **La Ferrassie**: The Aurignacian at La Ferrassie begins in Layer 7, directly overlying the Châtelperronian (Layer 6). [@Talamo_La_Ferrassie_2020] classify this as Early Aurignacian (Aur-P1) based on carinated scrapers and wide Aurignacian blades. No split-base bone points (Proto-Aurignacian diagnostic) were found [@Delporte_1984_Ferrassie; @Talamo_La_Ferrassie_2020]. Layer 7b has mixed Early/Recent Aurignacian components.
- **Mladeč**: The ~20 lithic artifacts include only one carinated end scraper. The 40 bone points with massive bases ("Mladeč-type") lack split bases and occur stratigraphically above split-based points at other Central European sites, placing them in the Evolved Aurignacian (Aur-P2) [@Oliva_2006]. Direct dates of ~31 ka ¹⁴C BP (~35–36 cal BP) are too young for Proto-Aurignacian [@Wild_et_al_2005].
- **Vogelherd**: Riek's 1931 excavation removed 500 m³ in 12 weeks with no screening, using large horizontal spits that did not follow geological horizons. Documented mixing includes 38 refit connections between Aurignacian layers IV and V, Neolithic burials disturbing the southwestern area, and ~2–3% of tools in the Aurignacian layers potentially deriving from other periods [@Schurch_Conard_2026_reassess].

Because these attributions are important for the two-phase framework, this section tests the sensitivity of the network results to (A) reverting to the purely date-based assignment used in earlier analyses , each object assigned to a phase by its calibrated date alone , and (B) excluding Vogelherd entirely, given its documented stratigraphic mixing.

```{r}
# ── Analysis A: revert to purely date-based assignment ─────────────────────
# Reassign each object purely by its calibrated date (technology overrides
# removed); the Spy/El Castillo exclusions from the baseline are retained.
signbase_date <- signbase_full_clean %>%
  mutate(time_period2 = time_period_date,
         phase2 = ifelse(time_period_date %in% c("proto_aurignacian", "early_aurignacian"),
                         "Aur-P1", "Aur-P2"))

lat_long_date <- signbase_date %>%
  dplyr::select(site_name, longitude, latitude) %>%
  distinct(site_name, .keep_all = TRUE)

aurp1_date <- make_phase2_data("Aur-P1", signbase_date, lat_long_date)
aurp2_date <- make_phase2_data("Aur-P2", signbase_date, lat_long_date)

date_stats <- bind_rows(
  network_stats(extract_artifact(aurp1_date), threshold = 0.2) %>% mutate(Phase = "Aur-P1"),
  network_stats(extract_artifact(aurp2_date), threshold = 0.2) %>% mutate(Phase = "Aur-P2")
) %>%
  mutate(Condition = "Date-based") %>%
  dplyr::select(Phase, Condition, n_sites, n_edges, density, mean_degree,
                transitivity, modularity)

# ── Analysis B: exclude Vogelherd entirely ─────────────────────────────────
# s8_novog is precomputed by sensitivity_summary() in the s7-setup chunk
no_vog_stats <- excl$s8_novog
```

## S8.2 Results

```{r}
#| label: tbl-reclass-comparison
#| tbl-cap: "Network statistics under three conditions: baseline (technology-based assignment), date-based (each object assigned purely by calibrated radiocarbon date, with the Spy/El Castillo exclusions retained), and exclude Vogelherd (technology-based baseline with the site of Vogelherd removed entirely). Threshold = 0.2, Jaccard similarity."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom

baseline_reclass <- bind_rows(
  network_stats(aurp1_artifact_data, threshold = 0.2) %>% mutate(Phase = "Aur-P1"),
  network_stats(aurp2_artifact_data, threshold = 0.2) %>% mutate(Phase = "Aur-P2")
) %>%
  mutate(Condition = "Baseline (technology-based)") %>%
  dplyr::select(Phase, Condition, n_sites, n_edges, density, mean_degree, transitivity, modularity)

all_reclass <- bind_rows(baseline_reclass, date_stats, no_vog_stats)

kable(all_reclass,
      col.names = c("Phase", "Condition", "Sites", "Edges", "Density",
                    "Mean degree", "Transitivity", "Modularity"),
      digits = 3,
      align = "lllcccccc")
```

```{r}
# ── Inline helpers for prose ────────────────────────────────────────────────
s8_md <- function(ph, cond) round(all_reclass$mean_degree[all_reclass$Phase == ph & all_reclass$Condition == cond], 2)
s8_ns <- function(ph, cond) all_reclass$n_sites[all_reclass$Phase == ph & all_reclass$Condition == cond]
s8_ne <- function(ph, cond) all_reclass$n_edges[all_reclass$Phase == ph & all_reclass$Condition == cond]
s8_mo <- function(ph, cond) round(all_reclass$modularity[all_reclass$Phase == ph & all_reclass$Condition == cond], 3)
```

### Effects by condition

**Date-based alternative (Analysis A).** Reverting to purely date-based criteria changes the membership of three sites. Mladeč moves from Aur-P2 to Aur-P1 (its ~35–36 ka BP (calibrated) dates fall in the Early Aurignacian range, which is folded into Aur-P1), while Hohle Fels and Vogelherd are split across the phases by object date: `r excl$hf_p1` of `r nrow(signbase_full_clean %>% filter(site_name == "Hohle Fels"))` Hohle Fels objects and `r excl$vog_p1_date` of `r nrow(signbase_full_clean %>% filter(site_name == "Vogelherd"))` Vogelherd objects remain in Aur-P1, and `r excl$hf_p2` and `r excl$vog_p2_date` objects , those calibrated to ~32 ka BP or younger , move to Aur-P2. The date-based assignment therefore fragments long-occupied sites whose assemblages span the phase boundary, which is precisely the failure mode the technology-based attribution is designed to avoid. Under this assignment Aur-P1 grows to `r s8_ns("Aur-P1", "Date-based")` sites and `r s8_ne("Aur-P1", "Date-based")` edges (mean degree `r s8_md("Aur-P1", "Date-based")`), while Aur-P2 , now missing Mladeč but containing `r excl$young_total` young-dated objects from Hohle Fels and Vogelherd , has `r s8_ns("Aur-P2", "Date-based")` sites and `r s8_ne("Aur-P2", "Date-based")` edges (mean degree `r s8_md("Aur-P2", "Date-based")`).

**Vogelherd exclusion (Analysis B).** Removing Vogelherd's `r nrow(signbase_full_clean %>% filter(site_name == "Vogelherd"))` objects from the technology-based baseline reduces Aur-P1 from `r s8_ns("Aur-P1", "Baseline (technology-based)")` to `r s8_ns("Aur-P1", "Exclude Vogelherd")` sites and from `r s8_ne("Aur-P1", "Baseline (technology-based)")` to `r s8_ne("Aur-P1", "Exclude Vogelherd")` edges. Mean degree falls from `r s8_md("Aur-P1", "Baseline (technology-based)")` to `r s8_md("Aur-P1", "Exclude Vogelherd")` (`r paste0("−", excl$md_pct, "%")`), and modularity from `r s8_mo("Aur-P1", "Baseline (technology-based)")` to `r s8_mo("Aur-P1", "Exclude Vogelherd")`. Aur-P2 is unaffected (`r s8_md("Aur-P2", "Exclude Vogelherd")`, `r s8_ne("Aur-P2", "Exclude Vogelherd")` edges, `r s8_ns("Aur-P2", "Exclude Vogelherd")` sites).

## S8.3 Phase-Ordering Robustness

The most consequential finding is that **the Aur-P1 > Aur-P2 connectivity ordering is preserved under every condition**:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-s8-ordering
```
